title: High-risk medicines and medication errors
blurb: Give insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, potassium and methotrexate safely, and respond openly when a medication error happens.
question: A patient's new inpatient chart shows methotrexate 10 mg once daily for rheumatoid arthritis. Her GP record shows 10 mg once weekly. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: High-risk medicines are those where an error is more likely to cause serious harm or death: insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, concentrated potassium, methotrexate and high-strength midazolam are classic examples. Several wrong-dose or wrong-selection errors with them are Never Events: incidents judged wholly preventable because strong national barriers exist. Knowing the barrier is the key to preventing the error.
teach.cite: NHS England Never Events list 2018 (updated February 2021)

teach.h: Medication Never Events and their barriers
head: Never Event
Barrier you apply
rows: Mis-selection of strong potassium (10% w/v or more) given IV
Use ready-mixed bags; concentrate kept in pharmacy or critical care, locked away from diluents
Insulin syringe or pen; never draw insulin from a pen into a syringe
Weekly dose checked; patient leaflet and monitoring record
Use 1 mg/mL; 2 mg/mL and 5 mg/mL restricted to specific areas
Oral or enteral medicine given parenterally
Oral/enteral syringes that cannot fit IV ports

items.label: insulin overdose when 'u' is read as a 0

teach.body: Measure insulin with an insulin syringe or an insulin pen, write 'units' in full, and never withdraw insulin from a pen or cartridge with a syringe (NPSA 2010; Patient Safety Alert 2016). If a conscious person who can swallow has a glucose below 4.0 mmol/L, give 15-20 g of quick-acting glucose, recheck, and repeat if there is no improvement after 15 minutes, then give a snack. If they are unresponsive, give nothing by mouth and get urgent help.
teach.cite: Never Events list 2018; RCUK First aid 2025

teach.caption: Check opioid doses against the person's previous exposure: a dose safe for a regular user can be dangerous for someone opioid-naive.

teach.body: Anticoagulants such as warfarin prevent clots but cause bleeding. Check monitoring (for warfarin, the INR) before giving a dose, watch for bleeding or bruising, and look for interactions: ibuprofen adds to bleeding risk and St John's wort reduces warfarin's effect (BNF). A very high INR is a reason to withhold the dose and inform the prescriber urgently. Transcribing anticoagulants needs particular care (RPS/RCN 31).

teach.caption: NICE NG5 1.1.7: report all medicines-related patient safety incidents consistently and in a timely way. Near misses are reported too.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Nurse Tamsin and Edna
teach.body: Preparing the 14:00 round, Tamsin sees Edna, 88, prescribed oral morphine 50 mg four-hourly. Edna is opioid-naive. The dose looks ten times too high, so Tamsin withholds it, contacts the prescriber to have it corrected, and reports a near miss. Later she notices Irene's chart shows methotrexate 10 mg once DAILY while her GP record says once WEEKLY. She withholds it, contacts the prescriber urgently and checks that no daily doses have already been given.

teach.text: 'U' and 'IU' are banned for insulin because a scrawled 'U' looks like a 0 and turns 10 units into 100. Write 'units' in full. Similarly, methotrexate for arthritis or psoriasis is WEEKLY; a daily prescription is a red flag to stop and check.

items: Insulin: 'units' in full, insulin syringe or pen, never draw from a pen; treat glucose below 4.0 mmol/L with 15-20 g quick-acting glucose.
Potassium: use ready-mixed bags; strong concentrate is restricted and locked away from diluents.
Methotrexate (non-cancer) is weekly; query any daily prescription.
Opioid toxicity: call for help, support breathing, give prescribed naloxone; check doses in opioid-naive people.
After an error: make safe, inform, be open, report (including near misses), learn.

summary: You can now apply the national barriers for insulin, potassium, methotrexate, midazolam and anticoagulants and respond to opioid toxicity and hypoglycaemia. You can also act correctly after a medication error or near miss.

A.q: Agnieszka, 52, has brought her insulin pen into hospital. Her lunchtime dose is due, but the ward has run out of pen needles. A colleague suggests drawing the dose from the pen with an insulin syringe. What should the nurse do?
options: Obtain pen needles from pharmacy or another ward and give it
Draw it up with an insulin syringe, as the dose drawn up is the same
Draw it up with a standard 1 mL syringe and needle instead
Omit the dose and record that no pen needles were available
A.why: Withdrawing insulin from a pen or cartridge with a syringe is a Never Event (Patient Safety Alert 2016). Pen needles should be obtained so the pen is used as intended.

whyNot.1: Drawing insulin from a pen with any syringe is the specific error the alert prohibits.
whyNot.2: A non-insulin syringe is an incorrect device and risks a major overdose.
whyNot.3: Omitting insulin risks hyperglycaemia when the right equipment can be obtained.

A.q: Rhys, 68, takes gliclazide and insulin. Before lunch he feels shaky and sweaty. His capillary glucose is 3.2 mmol/L. He is alert and can swallow. What should the nurse do first?
options: Give his lunchtime insulin and then a meal
Recheck the glucose again in an hour before taking any action
Give IM glucagon and call the medical team
Give 15-20 g of quick-acting glucose and recheck
A.why: A conscious person who can swallow with glucose below 4.0 mmol/L is given 15-20 g quick-acting glucose, rechecked, and treated again if no improvement after 15 minutes, then a snack (RCUK first aid).

whyNot.0: Insulin would lower his glucose further.
whyNot.2: He is alert and can swallow, so oral quick-acting glucose is the first step.

A.q: Which prescription for insulin is written safely?
options: Insulin aspart 6u with meals
Insulin aspart 6 IU with meals
Insulin aspart 6 units with meals
Insulin aspart 6 IU (international) with meals
A.why: The word 'units' must be written in full; abbreviations such as 'u' or 'IU' have caused 10-fold overdoses (NPSA 2010; Never Events list).

whyNot.0: 'u' can be misread as a zero, turning 6 into 60.
whyNot.1: 'IU' is also an abbreviation that can be misread.
whyNot.3: Writing 'international' beside IU still uses the abbreviation; 'units' must be written in full.

B.q: Brian, 79, is difficult to rouse 2 hours after IV morphine. He has pinpoint pupils, a respiratory rate of 7 and SpO2 of 89% on air. What should the nurse do?
options: Call for help, support his breathing and give the prescribed naloxone
Let him sleep it off and recheck all of his observations in an hour's time
Give a further dose of morphine as he may be in pain
Sit him upright and give him a cup of strong coffee to help rouse him
B.why: These are signs of opioid toxicity with respiratory depression: call for help, open and support the airway and breathing with oxygen, and give naloxone as prescribed, with close monitoring.

whyNot.1: A respiratory rate of 7 with low saturation needs immediate action.
whyNot.2: More opioid would deepen the respiratory depression.
whyNot.3: Oral fluids are unsafe in a drowsy person and do not reverse opioids.

B.q: Jorge, 61, is prescribed potassium chloride 40 mmol in 1 litre of 0.9% sodium chloride IV over 8 hours. The ward has no ready-mixed bags, and a colleague suggests adding concentrate from the critical care unit. What should the nurse do?
options: Add the concentrate to a 1 litre bag and invert it to mix thoroughly
Give the dose orally as tablets without asking
Give the concentrate as a slow IV bolus instead
Obtain a ready-mixed bag from pharmacy or another area per policy
B.why: Strong potassium concentrate is restricted to pharmacy and critical care areas, and mis-selection is a Never Event. Ready-mixed infusions should be obtained.

whyNot.0: Adding concentrate on a general ward bypasses the national barrier.
whyNot.1: Changing route without a prescription is not permitted.
whyNot.2: Concentrated potassium as a bolus can cause fatal arrhythmia.

B.q: Hamid, 74, takes warfarin for a mechanical heart valve. His INR today is 8.5 (target 2.5-3.5). He has no bleeding. His evening dose is due. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the usual dose, as he has no signs of bleeding
Give half the usual dose tonight and recheck the INR next week
Withhold the warfarin and inform the prescriber urgently
Give the dose with vitamin K tablets from stock
B.why: An INR far above target greatly increases bleeding risk. The dose is withheld and the prescriber informed urgently so treatment can be decided.

whyNot.0: Absence of bleeding now does not make a further dose safe.
whyNot.1: Dose changes are the prescriber's decision, and a week is too long.
whyNot.3: Vitamin K needs a prescription and clinical decision.

C.q: Irene, 72, has rheumatoid arthritis. Her new inpatient chart shows methotrexate 10 mg once daily in the regular section. Her GP record shows 10 mg once weekly on Mondays. What should the nurse do?
options: Give today's dose, as it matches the dose in milligrams
Change the chart to weekly herself to match the GP record
Give it daily as written, as the hospital chart is the current record
Withhold it and contact the prescriber urgently to clarify
C.why: Methotrexate for non-cancer conditions is weekly; a dose above the intended weekly dose is a Never Event. Withhold, clarify urgently and check whether any doses have already been given.

whyNot.0: Matching milligrams does not make the frequency safe.
whyNot.1: Altering a prescription is prescribing, not a nursing action.
whyNot.2: Daily methotrexate risks a fatal overdose.

C.q: Nurse Ola realises she gave Leon, 45, 10 mg of oral morphine instead of the prescribed 5 mg 20 minutes ago. Leon is alert with a respiratory rate of 16. What should she do?
options: Monitor him, inform the prescriber, tell Leon and report it
Keep it to herself, as he is alert and seems unaffected by it
Omit his next dose to balance out the error
Record 5 mg on the chart to match the prescription
C.why: After an error, make the person safe (observe for toxicity), inform the prescriber, be open with the person, and report it so the system can learn (NMC Code 14; NICE NG5).

whyNot.1: Concealing an error breaches the duty of candour and may leave harm undetected.
whyNot.2: Omitting doses without a prescriber's decision is another error.
whyNot.3: Recording a false dose is falsification of records.

C.q: Preparing a round, Nurse Tamsin sees Edna, 88, prescribed oral morphine 50 mg four-hourly. Edna is opioid-naive and her usual analgesia is paracetamol. What should Tamsin do?
options: Give the dose, as the prescription is the prescriber's own responsibility
Withhold it, have the prescription corrected and report a near miss
Give 5 mg instead, as that is probably what the prescriber meant
Give the dose and monitor her breathing closely
C.why: A nurse is accountable for what she administers and must raise concerns about a prescription before giving it. The error is caught before harm, so it is reported as a near miss.

whyNot.0: Nurses are accountable for their own actions and omissions when administering.
whyNot.2: Giving a different dose from the prescription is unlawful, however likely the intention.
whyNot.3: Giving a likely tenfold overdose to an opioid-naive person risks serious harm.

reteach.title: Small marks, big doses
reteach.question: How can a single letter or a single word on a chart cause a fatal error?

blocks.body: A 'u' becomes a zero. A 'weekly' becomes a 'daily'. An ampoule of strong potassium looks like sodium chloride. A pen cartridge holds far more insulin per mL than a syringe expects. Each barrier (writing 'units', checking methotrexate frequency, using ready-mixed potassium, using the right device) closes one of these gaps. When something looks unusual, stop and check before giving.

blocks.h: Something looks unusual on the chart

children.edge: Dose, frequency or unit looks wrong
children.label: Withhold and contact prescriber

blocks.text: A near miss (error caught before it reaches the patient) is still reported. That is how barriers get stronger.

explain.body: 'Units' in full; insulin syringe or pen; never withdraw from a pen with a syringe; check glucose and food intake.

test.q: Which practice with insulin is listed as a Never Event?
options: Giving insulin with a meal
Rotating injection sites
Checking capillary blood glucose before each dose
Withdrawing insulin from a pen with a syringe
test.why: The Never Events list includes withdrawing insulin from an insulin pen or refill and giving it with a syringe and needle.

whyNot.0: Giving mealtime insulin with food is normal practice.
whyNot.2: Glucose checks are part of safe practice.

explain.body: Strong potassium (10% w/v or more) is restricted to pharmacy and critical care, locked away from diluents. General wards use ready-mixed infusions.

test.q: Where should concentrated potassium chloride ampoules be stored, according to the NPSA alert?
options: On every ward, next to the 0.9% sodium chloride used for flushes
In pharmacy and critical care areas that need them urgently
In the ward CD cupboard with opioids
In the emergency trolley on every ward
test.why: The alert restricts concentrate to pharmacy and critical care areas where needed urgently, in a separate locked cupboard away from common diluents.

whyNot.0: Storing next to diluents is how mis-selection happens.
whyNot.2: General ward storage, even locked, bypasses the restriction.
whyNot.3: Emergency trolleys on every ward would spread the risk.

explain.body: Non-cancer methotrexate is weekly; any dose above the intended weekly dose is a Never Event. Conscious sedation uses 1 mg/mL midazolam; 2 and 5 mg/mL are restricted.

test.q: Which midazolam strength should be used for conscious sedation outside specialist areas?
options: 1 mg/mL
2 mg/mL
5 mg/mL
10 mg/mL
test.why: Low-strength midazolam (1 mg/mL) is used for conscious sedation; high strengths (2 mg/mL and 5 mg/mL) are restricted to areas such as anaesthesia, ICU and palliative care.

whyNot.1: 2 mg/mL is a high strength restricted to specific areas.
whyNot.2: 5 mg/mL is a high strength restricted to specific areas.
whyNot.3: 10 mg/mL is not the recommended sedation strength.

explain.body: Make safe, inform the prescriber and nurse in charge, be open with the person, report (including near misses), and learn in a fair-blame culture.

test.q: A nurse spots a wrong dose on a chart and stops it before it is given. What should happen next?
options: Take no further action, as no harm reached the patient
Tell the patient's family to monitor the chart
Have it corrected and report it as a near miss
Correct the dose on the chart herself
test.why: Near misses are reported so systems can learn (NICE NG5 1.1.7 asks for all medicines-related incidents to be reported). The prescriber corrects the prescription.

whyNot.0: Unreported near misses hide weak barriers.
whyNot.1: Monitoring the chart is the professionals' responsibility.
whyNot.3: Changing a prescription is prescribing, not a nursing action.
